utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Russo, are you ready to continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the usher is already trying to find the witness to escort him to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tchernetsky.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Russo will now continue his examination. Pease proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, we left off yesterday at a discussion or attempting to start a discussion about the shelling in the Cetina area in July of 1995. Do you recall those incidents?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could ask, Mr. Registrar, to please pull up 65 ter number 4938.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: While that is being pulled up, Mr. Tchernetsky, I'll tell you that we've tried to enlarge portions of the map which was admitted yesterday. That was Exhibit P206.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That was Exhibit P206, if we could maybe make that a bigger. If I could ask for the assistance of the court usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I would like to have you, please, circle the area which you indicated in your witness statement that was being shelled in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like it tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further markings to be made on this section.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, may I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P207, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is part of a map marked by the witness, and is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, can you please explain to the Court what the Operation Harvest was and how it came about?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, there was shelling of the Cetina area, particularly when the harvesting began, when the season began. The Serbian leadership, the Serbian authorities, approached the HQ of the UNPROFOR, protesting against the shelling and asking for assistance in preventing further shelling, because it didn't allow peasants to harvest. As soon as the machinery came out into the field, shelling began from the side of Bosnia. In order for peasants to be able to harvest, we organised a joint operation; that is, joint between monitors from the Sector South and the civilian police of the UN. How did we do this? On a daily basis, we allocated one patrol in a vehicle that bore a flag visibly, and this patrol helped people harvest. We monitored any appearance of weaponry, including tanks, from the Bosnian side; but while we were there, there was no shelling. One patrol would work until lunch-time; and after lunch-time, it would be the civilian UN police. We rotated. This operation lasted for a week, maybe a little longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Prior to the time that you began this mission, had you been to the Cetina valley area before?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That area was in our area of responsibility, and we regularly patrolled it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether or not you or your UNMO teams ever experienced restriction of movement patrolling in the Cetina area?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the area of the Cetina, the Serbian authorities did not put up any obstacles to our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you please give the Court an idea of what the Cetina valley looks like. How big is the area that was being shelled?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this valley could have been two or three kilometres in length, and houses were laid out on both sides; in fact, three sides, west, north, and east. And in the centre, there was a large field. As for dimensions, as far as I know, before Operation Storm, there were about 1500 people living in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Then are you able to tell the Court whether or not this area was predominantly Serb or predominantly Croat?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were only Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court exactly what was being shelled. Where did you find evidence of shelling?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. The question what was being shelled, as opposed what's the evidence of the shelling. So those are two different issues. I assume he wasn't there when the shelling took place, so he doesn't what was being shelled. If he is talking about evidence, that is a different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, if you take it step by step, what was shelled and then on what evidence, or what evidence the witness may have found which led him to the conclusion that that area was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, my only footnote to that is that, I think, the witness stated he wasn't there when any shelling took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes you find evidence even if you are not there --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping Speakers] ... no. I understand, Judge. In fact, that was the second part of my question prior to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, can you tell the Court if you ever saw any evidence of shelling in the Cetina valley?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did observe aftermath of shelling in Cetina valley; and at least two times, I personally went out into the field to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Court what exactly what it is you saw that lead you to believe that shelling had occurred?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went out on assignment by the HQ of the sector, to investigate after instances of shelling. We observed the craters, we found traces of shrapnel, and we observed traces of shrapnel on houses and on cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether or not, during any of the times you went to the Cetina valley, if there were any ARSK weapons deployed in the area?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area that I indicated on the map, not a single of our patrols found any weaponry or artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether or not there were any ARSK troop positions in the areas that were being shelled?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the entire duration of my field missions into that area, I only once saw a soldier who said he was on leave in the area of Cetina. He was unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether, during your patrols or the patrols of your UNMO team, you found anything of military significance in the Cetina valley?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area that I indicated, there was no weaponry, artillery, or ordnance, or troops. The closest weaponry was several kilometres away in the area of Kijevo, and further on, closer to the confrontation line, to the south of Cetina, maybe six or eight kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tchernetsky, you just mentioned the name of a place called "Kijevo." If you could please look at your screen, there is a Kijevo indicated to the top left side. Is that the place that you're talking about? You don't have to circle it. I'm just asking if that's it.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's here. It's to the west, north-west of Cetina several kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what exactly was there at Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly; but in the area of Kijevo, as far as I remember, we saw a piece of artillery, a rocket launcher in position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tchernetsky, if the ARSK had fired from the area of your team's responsibility into an area controlled by the HV or by other Croat forces, is that something that your UNMO team would have been tasked to investigate?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would depend on the area targeted because the sector was divided into areas of responsibilities among various groups of UNMO monitors. And on the Croatian side, we also had two of our groups, one in Sinj and one in Sibenik. If a territory was targeted that was in their area of responsibility, it was their job to investigate. But if the shelling was from the Serbian side by Serbian artillery, in our area of responsibility, then it was our job to investigate, to find out where exactly the shelling came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether or not you were ever tasked to investigate shelling by the ARSK in the Cetina valley?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand the question. Do you mean that the area of Cetina was being targeted by ARSK, by the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I think you misunderstood my question. What I was asking is if you had ever been tasked to investigate shelling by the ARSK coming from the Cetina valley, firing across into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, at least not while I was on mission among the UNMOs. We did not get any such assignments from the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I think my question was a little more specific than I should have asked. Did you or your UNMO team ever investigate any shelling by the ARSK, coming from the Cetina valley to any other area.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, and I was an ordinary monitor at the time, there were no such investigations, at least not by our group of monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm going to move to another topic. I don't know whether or not you wanted to ask any questions on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, I'd like to move now to a discussion of the events in the area of Strmica prior to Operation Storm. I believe you discussed this in your first witness statement. That would be P204 at page 2, paragraph 4. In that paragraph, you indicated you had gone quite often to the area of Strmica to investigate cases of artillery fire by the Croatian side. Can you please tell the Court approximately how many times you went to Strmica to investigate the area being shelled?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To investigate shelling, I went there at least twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, again, if you could, for the benefit of the Court, explain what evidence you found, if any, that shelling had occurred in that area.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, we found craters from explosions of shells. We found partially destroyed buildings, destroyed by shelling, with traces of shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what kinds of things were affected or hit by this kind of shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Residential houses were damaged; and in the course of one investigation, I personally noticed there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. None of this information about what was hit and houses, et cetera, concerning Strmica is anywhere in any the statements or proofing notes, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, his witness statement indicates that the area of Strmica was shelled, and that there were no military positions. I don't think it is a stretch to ask the witness what exactly was hit by the shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there are roads going through Strmica, there are other facilities going Strmica. There is nothing in any of these that beg the question that counsel just asked, that civilian houses in some fashion was hit, or, better still, that this witness had been any crater analysis while he was there. There is nothing in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No military purpose. The question was quite open. What kind of things. There could have been roads. So I think this is a type of clarification Mr. Russo is entitled to ask. And if that causes any problems in cross-examination of the witness, we'll first hear his answers, then you may apply for further time. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Tchernetsky. It seems that you may have been cut off in the middle of an answer. I will ask you again to explain what kind of things were affected by the shelling.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that there had been shelling because we could observe craters from exploded shells. We could see residential houses, buildings, and a school building damaged by shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did your UNMO team ever experience any restriction of movement prior to Operation Storm in the area of Strmica?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The thing is that, in Strmica, there were positions of the Knin Battalion of the UNPROFOR on the edge of the area. It was the Kenyan Battalion, and neither we nor the troops of the UNPROFOR had any difficulty moving around the area. Our group of UNMOs regularly controlled that area, and would send out patrols on a daily base.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your witness statement, you discuss a specific incident of shelling in Strmica for which you were personally present, along with others. I would like to you please explain to the Court the circumstances of what happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the end of July. We received an assignment from the Sector HQ to investigate shelling that had occurred during the night, targeting the residential area of Strmica. This investigation was performed at the request of the ARSK command, and with cooperation of the military units of the army of RSK. We sent out two vehicles to Strmica; and before we reached the positions of the Kenyan Battalion, because, first of all, we wanted to hear their testimony about this since they had been in position at the time, shelling started against. It was a massive rocket and artillery attack. It was an artillery barrage from guns and mortars. We were forced to turn back, trying to exit the area targeted by artillery fire; but since shells started falling very close, we abandoned our vehicles and hid behind one of the houses nearby. The shelling continued for rather a long time as we were hiding in the basement of that house. As soon as it stopped a little, we reached our vehicles, trying to keep under cover and left quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please pull up 65 ter 4936.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: While that is pulling up Mr. Tchernetsky, I'll -- I'm going to tell you that is an aerial image of the area of Strmica, and I'm going to ask you to take a look at it and to please, if you're able, circle the areas which were being shelled on the day that you -- that you just testified about.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelling started when we were approximately here in this area. The first shells fell approximately here, to the west of the positions of the Kenyan Battalion. Then, a bit to the south -- you can remove this. All right. Then to the south, we were either here or here when we abandoned the vehicles and went downstairs into that basement. The shelling covered all this territory, like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tchernetsky, you indicated "here and here," where you may have abandoned the vehicles. Can I ask you to place an X at both of those spots where you believe you may have abandoned your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely, but it was roughly here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if you could, please, place a circle around the area where the KenBat position was.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kenyan Battalion was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if could you please label that small circle you just made with a "UN."

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have a map with a lot of circles and ovals. Let's try to see. I see that the witness testimony was that he was approximately at the place where he added "UN" to the map, when he first, I think, experienced shelling. He then indicated that to the west of that position, with the not-perfect circle, the highest, was what the area where the shelling --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first shells, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes, I'm just putting it on the record. That's where the first shells were. Then the circle further down within the oval shape was where subsequently the shells fell. Where we found a cross or an X, that's where the witness said he abandoned his vehicle, but he earlier indicated that it could have been also at the dot just north of that. And, finally, the witness indicated that in the whole area surrounded by an oval shape, that's where the shelling took place. Finally, the very small circle, UN, is where the KenBat was located. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then a number should be assigned, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this becomes Exhibit P208.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections? I see here no objection. P208 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, can you please tell Court whether during any of your previous investigations to the Strmica area or during the time that you experienced the shelling if there were any ARSK weapons in that area?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the Strmica area. We came across armaments and military units, those of the ARSK. They were to the south, a great deal to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Were there any ARSK troop positions or camps in that area of Strmica that was shelled?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not investigate the area that was shelled, so I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm asking in specific about the areas that you have just indicated where shells fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's what he just answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether the witness understood the last question. Did you investigate the areas you just circled, or do you say, "No, I've got no knowledge of any ARSK"? I think it was troops or positions there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said that in Strmica, in the residential neighbourhood of Strmica, we did not see any military units or armaments of the ARSK. And after the shelling, we did not investigate the areas that were to the west that provided support during the shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, the -- I believe you indicate that there were areas that were to the west that provided support during the shelling. What areas are you referring to? Are the areas to the west located on the image that you see before you here?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I said was that the areas that were subjected to shelling, that were targeted, we did not investigate that area. We did not visit that area. As for Strmica itself, in the residential area, there were neither military units nor weaponry of the ARSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I'm now confused by your answer. You're saying - and correct me if I'm wrong - the areas that you circled on this map were areas that were shelled while you were there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And are those the residential areas which you did not investigate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. There is quite a lot of confusion about the answers of the witness, so Mr. Russo is perfectly entitled to seek clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The areas that you have circled, are those the residential areas which you did not investigate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, it seems that you and your questions are adding to the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I think I asked the question incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, you have put two circles and an oval on that map. That's where you said the shells fell. Are those the residential areas you mentioned or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not claiming that those were residential areas. We saw explosions in that area; but as for what was located there, I really couldn't tell you anything about that. We did not investigate the impact, the results of the shelling of that particular shelling because we eye-witnessed that shelling, and we simply went back to the headquarters and reported about very intense shelling of the Strmica area with rocket artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, please. Yes, that's clear now. In the very beginning of your answer, when you said it was in the end of July, you said you received an assignment from the sector headquarters to investigate shelling that had occurred during the night, targeting the residential area of Strmica. When you went there, did you find out what was the residential area which caused you to be assigned to investigate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were sent to the area to the north of Strmica. By your leave, I will show it, I will indicate it. We were sent to this area here, to this area; but we didn't reach that area because another shelling started. I'm showing now the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The area that we had been sent to look into, it's to the north of Strmica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the area you never reached. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please mark that and put an R. Mr. Usher, could you perhaps assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There we have an R. Now, you said, in one of your other answers, you said: "I said that in Strmica, in the residential neighbourhood of Strmica, we did not see any military units or armaments of the ARSK." What area did you have in mind when you gave that answer, this same area or another area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Strmica area is a settlement, a populated area, that stretches down the road. If I can show that on the map, this is the Strmica area. And to us, Strmica was this whole area. Earlier, we had investigations in that area when there were incidents of shelling, and we found there craters and houses damaged by shells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you said in that area, you did -- this is the larger area. Could you please put an R and a 2 to that area you just circled.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you said you did not see any military units or armaments of the ARSK. Were you referring to your earlier investigations, or were you referring to the day you just described when you arrived to investigate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both during earlier investigations and on the day we arrived to investigate that particular shelling and were shelled ourselves. In this area, that I just circled and marked with R2, we did not see any armed military units of the RSK there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That answer appears, again, on page 13, line 20. I take it that is correct. Yes. Mr. Russo, since the map was presented by you and it just adds to what the witness earlier said, I suggest that you tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections? No Objections. Mr. Registrar, this map, again marked by the witness with different markings, would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P209, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P209 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm going to move now to another topic. I assume the Court has satisfied itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, I'd lake to now discuss your discovery or a discovery of two bodies in a house in Knin on or about the 12th of August. You discussed this in your statement -- your first statement. That is P204 at page 4 the second paragraph. Do you recall this incident?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Court the circumstances of how those bodies were discovered?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The owner of the house where our office was located and where UNMOs lived asked us to go and check the neighbouring house, which was right next door. It was an abandoned house. Because as she was passing by, she felt she sensed this stench. She used to know the tenants of that house, and she asked us to go in and check about -- to check what had caused this stench. Together with the Polish observer, I don't remember his name but he was a member of our team, we entered the house and we found there two corpses: One was in one room, sitting in an arm chair, shot, because we saw blood traces, shot in the head. The other corpse was located in the room next door, lying next to an open window. There was a terrible stench in the house. Corpses had been lying there for quite sometime, started decomposing. It was quite hot at the time. We came out of the house, following which I went to the headquarters and reported about the incident to our leaders. I was ordered to turn that incident over to the civilian police of the United Nations because that fell under the jurisdiction the military police of the UN, which was located in the same camp, and I reported this to them as well. After that, I went to patrol. As for what happened afterwards, my colleagues told me about it. The civilian police of the UN arrived, and then Croatian civilian police arrived to the site. They entered the house, following which the bodies were removed, and that's the whole story.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your second statement - that's P205 - at paragraph 17, you discuss attempts that you made to assist the relative of these diseased to obtain some evidence of their death. Can you please explain to the Court the efforts that you made in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of those who were killed was quite a wealthy person. His family, who had left the area during Operation Storm and fled to Belgrade, did not have any money left. They contacted me through some relatives, asking me to obtain some kind of evidence in order to declare the fact that this person had died and, thus, proceed with the inheritance. At that time, I was already a member of a different mission, since our mission was -- initial mission was terminated. I was on leave and I went to Zagreb, and all the documents from my initial mission were deposited in the archives. I was given permission to enter the premises of the archives in order to find documents that would confirm that these people had been found dead. However, when I entered the archives, I realised that a number of documents pertaining to the military observers, both in Podkonje which was our team, as well as the observers from the human rights team, in the period between August and October of 1995 were missing. All of these documents were missing. There were several boxes of documents that were missing, even though they were listed there and were supposed to be present in the archives. The clerk who worked in the archives, when asked by me about the whereabouts of these document, couldn't provide me with a reasonable answer. Following this, and knowing that the file was turned over to the civilian police of the United Nations, I tried to find some documents pertaining to that investigation in the archives of the civilian police. At that time, in Zagreb, we had a training team remaining there, a team that prepared the civilian police, that conducted training. There was an archive of the civilian police of Sector South within their premises. So I addressed the chief of that centre, and he allowed me to look for these documents. And as I was doing so, I found the documents which pertained to the events, the relevant events; rather, the box where the documents were supposed to be. The documents pertaining to events and investigation which took place in August of 1995. However, many documents, including the file on investigation, were missing. I just found the initial report of the leader of the civilian police who came there. There was just his initial report of that incident. I asked the permission of the chief of that centre and copied that document, and this is the document that you see before you. After that, I made --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please pull up document 65 ter 1754.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, is this the document that you found?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would tender this as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we need to check. I believe I used this document in cross-examination. It's been admitted through the testimony of Mr. Flynn. I think it is a Defence exhibit now. Let me double-check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, if you keep it in the back of your mind, then we wait a second to assign a number to it and first seek verification of whether it is already a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, while we're investigating that matter, I'd like to move to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, first, let me ask the Court if there are any questions regarding this incident. I'm going to move to another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, there is another matter. 84 and 85 are mentioned as items annexed to this supplemental witness statement. I think, however, that in confidential annex A and confidential annex B to the Prosecution submission of Rule 92 ter statements, we find three documents attached but not 84 and 85. Could you please verify whether that is the case or not. That is at least what reached us, and also perhaps something for the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, before we move on. Mr. Misetic is, in fact, correct. This document is D65.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it was -- again, Mr. Misetic is correct. It came in during the course of the testimony of Mr. Flynn on -- I don't have the exact date here. It must have been 7 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And for further clarification, Your Honour, this particular report is appended as AT-4 to the supplemental witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't find it, but I have got it now in front in hard copy. So we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was apparently not 7 August 2008, but 10 August 2008 that came in -- excuse me, April, 2008 that D68 came in. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This being clarified, Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I was going to move to another topic. I didn't know if the Court had any additional questions with regard to the discovery of the two bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, I would like to discuss now some of the things that you witnessed after Operation Storm. If I could direct your attention to the first statement - that is P204 - at page 3 in the last paragraph, where you discuss the incident of burning in Knin sometime between the 10th and the 12th of August of 1995. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if you could, please briefly explain to the Court exactly what happened on that day on what you observed.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, our group was still within the area of the headquarters -- or, rather, was using the premises of the headquarters. We did not have separate premises in Knin. Late one evening, we received information about the fact that an entire neighbourhood was on fire in Knin. I don't know where that information had come from. Perhaps somebody just saw it from the balcony of their building. I can't remember now exactly. Either I was given a task from Tennard [phoen], the Senior Military Observer of the sector, or I was perhaps given assignment from our team leader to go out and investigate the fire. We went to investigate together with my Norwegian colleague, Tor Munkelien, and another person asked to join us. He was an English journalist, Alun Roberts. We set out. But as we reached the centre of Knin, we were halted there because there was -- the road was blocked by police cars, and we were stopped there. And even though we had all the valid observer papers, they did not allow us to move through. Croatian policemen ordered us to turn back. We were escorted by two vehicles of Croatian police back to our camp. After that, we decided to go back to the fire, the area that was on site, and check out what was going on there. We left Alun Roberts there, and Tor and myself went back into our patrol vehicle and left the camp. As we left our compound, there was a Croatian police car waiting for us there. They started escorting us. We did not drive towards north, towards Knin, but rather to the south, to Drnis. Croatian police moved away, drove away. We made a U-turn, and went back to Knin. I was familiar with the area. We asked for directions. We came back to the area arriving from the north and reached the site that was on fire. The entire neighbourhood was practically on fire. There were several fire engines there and fire brigade teams. There was several police cars, as well. But what shocked was that none of them did anything to put the fire out. Tor made several photographs while I distracted the police, manoeuvring in the car and making them believe that we were lost, that we had lost our way and asking for directions. During that time, Tor managed to make some photos, and then we continued on our way. He gave our photos to the British reporter, Alun Roberts; and, as far as I know, these photos were later published.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could 65 ter number 4881 brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Is this the document that is referenced as Annex AT-3 in paragraph 16 of your second statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if you could --

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If you could please explain to the Court what the markings on this photograph mean.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first mark is the location of our team after we were finally able to organise our own office. Number 2 is the point where Tor, Alun Roberts, and I were stopped on our first attempt to reach Knin. The dotted line is the route we moved along from the camp to the point where we were stopped and turned back. The other dotted line is the route -- the roundabout way towards Knin, the site of the fire. Number 3 is the fire. It is very hard to be more precise now, but it is approximately there, in the area of the northern settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tchernetsky.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would tender the exhibit. I don't know if I have any specific questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No specific questions. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P210, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P210 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, this incident of burning is not reported in any of the UNMO sitreps. Can you explain why that might be?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say why. I was an ordinary monitor. I did my job. Why it wasn't reflected in reports, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Do you recall making a report of this incident to your HQ?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were, our team, was directly at the headquarters. We worked in the same place as the HQ of the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move now to your first statement - that's P204, page 4 - the third paragraph where you discuss a special police mop-up operation in the Plavno valley area. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like you to please try and locate this area on one of the other maps you provided with your second statement, and we will take it in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to have, as yesterday, the entire map admitted, and then we will have enlarged sections of it for the Court's benefit. Mr. Registrar, if we could then have 65 ter number 4879.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's my map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And is it the map that you provided as AT-1 in your second statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would tender 4879.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. No one jumps up. Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P211, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P211 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please now have 65 ter 4939.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, the area indicated here in this enlargement, you can see a Plavno written quite large towards the bottom, and there's a Palanka toward the top as you directly north. Is this the area that you discuss regarding the mop-up operation?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this as an exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, I take it? Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P212, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P212 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, can you please explain to the Court what your understanding of what these mop-up operations was at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we were informed about two mop-up operations, one in the Dinara mountain range area, and the other in Plavno. What exactly was a mop-up operation? The area was blocked. All exits from that area would be blocked. And after that, the area would be combed, both population centres would be combed, as well as the entire territory. From what I know from local residents, they were ordered, all the remaining population and that was not much, was ordered to stay within their settlements because anyone found outside a settlement would be killed, liquidated. In that way, Croatian army troops would mop up areas, searching for remaining ARSK soldiers or any other military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I think you've already indicated as part of your answer, but I want to be clear about what your source of information for this understanding was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Which understanding is that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The understanding that the population was ordered to stay, or the understanding that people would be liquidated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you please be more precise, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. I will take it one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, you indicated that during a mop-up operation, the area would be blocked, all exits from the area would be blocked. Where did that piece of information come from?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it from my own eyes. I know it from my own experience when such an operation was carried out in the Dinara mountain range area and in the Plavno area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You also indicated that the entire area which was blocked off would be combed, including the population centres, as well as the entire territory. Where did that information come from?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first such information I received from our Sector HQ; that is, the Sector South. The HQ got that information from Croatian authorities. They said that within a given time-frame for a certain period, the area would be blocked off, due to a special mop-up operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And your understanding that within the area blocked off, the remaining inhabitants would be ordered to stay within their settlements and anyone found outside of those settlements would be killed, or I believe you used the term "liquidated." Where did that information come from?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something we learned from local residents who told us about it. Local residents were warned not to leave their homes and not to leave their towns or villages during a mop-up operation. That's something we learned from the people themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And specifically about the fact that people not found in those areas would be killed, where did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same source. Local residents said they were warned to that effect by Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And the final thing I would like to discuss would be the discovery of the ARSK soldiers in the area of Podinarje that you explain at pages 4 and 5 of your first statement. That's P204.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter number 4937.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, looking at the enlarged area on the screen, is this generally the area that you referenced, about where you found these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it there are no objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P213, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P213 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tchernetsky, in your first statement, this is at page 5 in the first paragraph, you indicated that, initially, you decided not to report the discovery of these soldiers, and that you gave them a map to try to help them escape do Bosnia. Let's be clear, as an UNMO, you're not supposed to do that, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's a leading question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think there is any dispute whether or not he is supposed to do that, but I can ask it in non-leading fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand he is trying to rehabilitate the witness in direct, but I think it is a little --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether he is trying to rehabilitate. Is there any dispute about whether it is within the mandate of an UNMO to provide maps to soldiers in order to help them to escape?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then this is agreed between the parties. The only thing is now whether the witness was aware of -- Were you aware that this was as the parties here think was not in accordance with your mandate as an UNMO to provide a soldier you find with a map in order to facilitate for him to escape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But at that moment, it was my first spontaneous reaction to assist people who were facing death, who were in danger, and I violated the mandate of UNMOs at that moment because I could not see any other way out if I wanted to help and save these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and thank you, Mr. Tchernetsky, for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, prior to this incident, were you ever given any instructions by anyone about what you were supposed to do when you find, or if you found, ARSK soldiers during your patrols?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to these soldiers after you helped negotiate their surrender?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the presence of representatives of other international organisations, we turned over those soldiers to Croatian authorities. After which, one of these soldiers, as far as I know, was let go and he was given release documents; whereas, others were convicted, and I know from my colleagues from the human rights team they were transferred from Knin to Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I please have Exhibit P138.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, if you will follow along with me here. This is an UNMO HQ sitrep from the 2nd of September which, I believe, according to your statement is several days after you negotiated the surrender of these soldiers. And you will notice that the highlights indicate that: "Croatian authorities continue to severely violate Geneva Convention towards POWs. Eight former ARSK soldiers, whose surrender was monitored by UNMOs on 28 August, continue to be kept in custody in Knin's school. They were traumatised. Some of them had clear signs of beating on their faces. See HRAT report 1 September." Were you at all involved in the HRAT which visited these soldiers at the Knin school?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I did not visit those soldiers myself. It was only the representatives of the human rights team who were able to do that, and the human rights team consisted of our monitors, UNMOs, and representatives of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Do you know which UNMOs from your team would have been assigned to the HRAT teams?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our team, Peter Marti, as vice-captain; and Ivo, I don't remember the last name, Czech captain, became part of the human rights team.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They visited those POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's best that we first take a break. Who will be the first one to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Could you give us any indication of how much time you will approximately need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Between an hour, hour and a half, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the other Defence teams -- Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I think I will probably require less time, and I would estimate three quarters of an hour at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Hour Honour. Obviously, it depends on how much is covered here, but I think it is approximately two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll first have a break. We'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the delay. I was kept in a meeting which took more time than expected and so I did not want it to be cancelled. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic who is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tchernetsky. I'd like you to refer to P204 which is your statement dated December -- excuse me, May 18th, 2002, page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And if the usher could call that up, I'm specifically referring to the third paragraph that starts, "Unfortunately ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, you were speaking earlier during direct examination, or almost left on direct examination, talking about mop-up operations. You said you had witnessed two mop-up operations during your time as an United Nations Military Observer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I witnessed one operation in the Podinarje area and the second one in Plavno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I want to refer to the one in Plavno that we talk about in P204. Before I get to that, you were an United Nations Military Observer from June 1995 till December of 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And in that entire time-frame, it's your testimony that you saw no more than two mop-up operations. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mop-up operations took place after Operation Storm; that is, in end August and September, as far as I know -- as far as can I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So you were aware that there were ongoing mop-up operations beginning at the end of August and through September of 1995 conducted by the special police of the Ministry of Interior. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to what units were directly involved in the operations, I don't know. The only time when I had personal contact of the unit involved in such an operation was in Podinarje, and that is reflected in my statement. I even named that man, Colonel Vrsaljko. He was commander of the special Zadar-Knin unit. Who conducted the operation in Plavno, which units, I cannot tell you. Because when we arrived with the human rights patrol - in fact, at that time, we are carrying humanitarian aid into Plavno - we were stopped at that entrance into that location. The two roads leading to it were blocked, and the military police soldiers manning the check-point told us that the area was closed, axis was denied, and we had to turn back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I was just trying to get to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tchernetsky. Do you know that the special police mop-up operations did not begin until on or about August 21st, 1995? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not informed of the commencement of these operations officially. The first time I had anything to do with it was when that RSK soldier was found in the area of Podinarje. In fact, soldiers were found, and I organised the process of turning them over to international organisations. At the time of the morning briefing, the senior UNMO warned us that Croatian authorities had officially warned him that there would be special mop-up operations in the area and the area would be blocked off. I cannot remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Tchernetsky. I know you have a tendency to want to explain your answers. If you would try as best as can you to limit your responses to the question I pose, then we can make these things go a little bit quicker. Okay?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Going back to P 204, page 4 in the paragraph that begins, "Unfortunately." From your statement, you start: "Unfortunately, I do not remember the date when the Croatian special police were conducting the mop-up operation in Plavno valley. We were on patrol when we discovered this fact." It is true that at least as far as you know this may have happened in August of 1995, correct? It didn't happen certainly before August 21st.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the dates. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You had stated in your earlier response that you were stopped at the crossing by military police?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What crossing were you stopped at?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the intersection of the main road with the village road, leading into Plavno valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, did you have a chance to observe that mop-up operation as it progressed, or did you just hear about it and then you were prevented from going into the area?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were simply not given the opportunity to stay in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You said you came back to the area of Plavno two or three days after you were stopped by the military police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, could we have the map on the screen, so that the witness can indicate where exactly the cross-roads are where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to that, Your Honour, but the maps aren't the best quality, so I didn't want to lose time doing that. But I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that we had a cutout of the Plavno area in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will find it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That is correct, Judge. I will locate the P number for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's P212.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, the map, P212, of Plavno from your map -- strike that. This is an excerpt of your map, P212. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to circle in blue where you say that you were stopped by the military police, with the assistance of the usher?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think we need the usher there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am afraid I wouldn't be able to do that because this intersection is somewhat south, to the south of the area shown here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So the intersection in which you were stopped was to the south of the area depicted in P12 [sic].

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the south of the shown area, this is where the intersection is. The main road goes from south to north, and the village road goes to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if we get the whole of the map on the screen. And, meanwhile, of course, Mr. Kuzmanovic, just proceed. When we get that map on the screen, we'll find the portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if this is too large for the ELMO or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, I think it is in evidence, and then we can enlarge, zoom in most likely on that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I don't think the zoom-in function will allow the resolution necessary to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see. If not, then bad luck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That map is P211, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If P211 could be put on the screen. Meanwhile, you may continue, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, we will wait for the P211 to get on the screen, and I will ask you some additional questions regarding this Plavno valley Croatian special police operation. You, yourself, came back to that area three days later and had you a conversation with a woman, an elderly woman, about her husband. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Is there any indication of what her name was? Do you have any recollection?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, and I didn't keep any notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: She had said that her -- she was trying to find her husband, and you and your colleague, Mr. Komper, tried to find the man, but you could not find him. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time, when we tried to locate him, we learned where he had gone. It was a settlement called Kozja Jama, ten to 15 kilometres to the north of Palanka. We found Kozja Jama. We found the only remaining men there. There was just one elderly man remaining in the settlement, together with his daughter. We learned that the man who had gone missing, indeed, came to see him on that day but went back. So the first time we went to patrol Kozja Jama area, we didn't manage to find him; but on the following day, Pavel Komper, as member of another patrol, went approximately to the area indicated by the woman. They had a shelter for sheep there; and in this shelter, they found a corpse, the corpse of the man who was killed; several sheep that had been killed; and a dog. Subsequently, they helped remove the body because it was impossible to reach that area in a vehicle. The body was carried away and turned over to the woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, none of this is contained in any sitrep, as far as you're aware. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. The report about the fact that a body of the killed man was found was mentioned. I remember that that report was mentioned among us. Your Honours, in the map that I'm seeing now, I can show the intersection where we were stopped, as we were attempting to reach the Plavno valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, I take it that the witness may mark that intersection where he was stopped --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with a blue marker, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Tchernetsky, with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And where you've circled on this particular map is the intersection of where you were stopped by the military police and were not allowed to proceed into Plavno. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we have a --

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Previously so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- number for this document? I'd like to tender it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, no objections, I take it. Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D217, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the parties, before I admit it into evidence, is Plavno just a valley or also a village, because sometimes where the text is put on the map, it takes the view of what might be under that marking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Plavno is a valley. That's a valley. Then around the valley, there are many hamlets that make up that area, the region, what we used to refer to as the Plavno valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer. D217 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm just trying to find out where I left off. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, where we left off was before you identified the area on the map was. It's fair to state that you have not seen a sitrep that contains any information about this incident in the Plavno valley. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that, and I'm not claiming that I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, just to perhaps you read the last answer the witness gave before he went back to the map; that is, "I can't say ..." at page 39, line 1. I'll read it to him. Mr. Tchernetsky, the last thing before we went back to this map and the intersection, Mr. Kuzmanovic asked you: "Mr. Tchernetsky, none of this is contained in any sitrep, as far as you're aware. Correct?". Then your answer was: "I can't say. The report about the fact that a body of the killed man was found was mentioned. I remember that that report was mentioned among us." That's where we left the witness. Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You, yourself, did not see the man. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him. I didn't see the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your colleague found the man; and as far as you know, that was the end of the situation, as your involvement was concerned. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleague, as member of the patrol team, found the corpse and helped in evacuating the body. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, there is no indication in your statement as -- as to how this gentleman was killed, other than there's a notation of found -- that he was found shot dead. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There is no evidence, as far as you know, of who may have shot him. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There are no witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, would you not, Mr. Tchernetsky, that to attribute this unnamed man's death to any Croatian military force, whether it is a special police, the military police, the Croatian military, would be speculation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the most likely version because at that time there was a mop-up operation going on, and there were no other people from outside in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, you have no names of anyone who may have been involved in this operation. You have no evidence of how this man was killed, other than he was shot. Don't you agree with me that it would be a complete guess to figure out whether it was the Croatian military, the Croatian special police, or any other person that might have shot this man?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly don't have any evidence that would show directly that he was killed by any units of the Croatian special police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness one question? When you said the report that a man was killed was -- that the killed man was found was mentioned, did you refer to a written report or that it was orally reported to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We provided written reports on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say "I remember that that report was mentioned among us," were you referring to a written report, or were you referring to what was orally reported to you? If you don't remember, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, did you report this incident to the civil police for investigation?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We informed our headquarters, the headquarters that was in charge of us. We informed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, I'd like to change topics here for a moment. I'd like to talk to you generally about your work as a UN Military Observer, and you're main task at the end of Operation Storm, according to your May 18th statement, P204, was to observe and report on violations of humanitarian law. Correct? I guess I will read it to you on page 3, in this centre page 3 of your statement, page 204.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could please pull that up Mr. Usher or Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry. The witness has hard copies of his thing. I don't know if that will make things quicker, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, do you see on page 3, just above the centre of the page, where it says that: "The main task of the military observers after Operation Storm were, one, to estimate the destruction caused by the Croatian military operation; two, to monitor the movement of the Croatian military units; three, registration of the Serb civilians who remained in the area; and, four, to provide humanitarian aid to the civilians in coordination with ICRC and UNHCR." Did you read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, you had a continuing obligation of impartiality as a United Nations Military Observer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, I think that the mandate that was given to UNMOs in Sector South, after the Operation Storm, was exhausted, and I was given the tasks that were just enumerated. When carrying out these tasks, we were, first and foremost, supposed to be guided by -- or, rather, our mission turned from a military mission into a humanitarian one, and that was our first and foremost guiding principle. We were to provide help to people, primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But had you a continuing obligation of impartiality, meaning that could you not take sides. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that was the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, the Chamber has considered to what extent it is assisted by going, again, through the impartiality. If there are any issues in relation to that, as we heard earlier this morning and not for the first time, that providing maps to a soldier is beyond the mandate, fine. We'll hear if there is any news on that matter. But to spend - I don't know how much time you had in mind - but to spend another five minutes on the impartiality of the mandate, required by the mandate, that at this moment doesn't seem to assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That was the last question on that issue, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I wasted the time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, about the modalities of how you would report after Operation Storm. On each day you conducted a patrol, who would choose the route? Would you choose it, would the HQ choose it? Could you explain to us how those patrols were set up?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our area of responsibility, there was several permanent itineraries or routes, and they were patrolled regularly. In addition to that, whenever there were some extraordinary events or circumstances or when we received information about them in area under our responsibility, then we would set up a separate patrol team. But if there were no additional tasks, if there was nothing extraordinary, then we would just patrol the routine previously established and planned routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. How did these previously planned and established planned routes get set up? Who was the person who set these routes up?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: These routes were defined by the team commander, and they needed to receive approval of the sector commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just focus on your team for the purposes of my questioning. You were on Team Podkonje. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And on a typical day, how would your team get its instructions on where to go and what to do, and how many people would go on those patrols?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, the group commander would, on the previous evening, define tasks, indicate routes; and then in the morning, upon receiving information from the headquarters, if there were no additional tasks, the patrols, after briefing, would set out on previously established routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How often would you visit a specific area? For example, how often would have you gone to Plavno over the course of your routes? Once a week, twice a month?
