utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the Operation Storm, once a week, not more often than that. After Operation Storm, after our mission became a more humanitarian one, in the Plavno area we found quite a large number of remaining Serb residents; and, periodically, perhaps two or three times a week, we would visit that area, in order to check on the situation there, and provide humanitarian assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So, at the end of your day when your patrol was done, would all the team members then present their observations to a duty officer, and then the duty officer would put together an UNMO report? If it's not that way, then --

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And, then, that UNMO report would be delivered to UNMO HQ in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And your HQ was actually in Knin itself, was it not, Team Podkonje?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then any significant event that you would determine would be significant would be reported in your report that would go to HQ, like burning of houses or if someone was killed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How many people at the end of the day would be gathered together on your team to put together the team report?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team report was written by the duty officer and handed over to the team commander. And as for our team, it numbered 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was your team commander?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They changed, the group commanders. For a while -- are you interested primarily in the period after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Operation Storm, for a while, it was Felix Anglada, a Spanish major; and then Peter Marti a Swiss military officer; and then following them, I was appointed group commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And, then, who was the superior to your group, meaning that did it go to a -- from the team leader, it went to whom? Who was the next person up the chain?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group commander reported to the Senior Military Observer from Sector South. At that time, it was the Norwegian Lieutenant-Colonel Steinar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the deputy military commander or deputy military observer, was that Mr. Ermolaev?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And he was the deputy essential after Operation Storm through most, if not all, of August. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: More likely in August, because he was transferred later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So at least at the time relevant to what we're talking about, mid-to the end of August, he was the deputy military observer behind Colonel Hjertnes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, at some point, Mr. Tchernetsky, all the UNMO teams were ordered to conduct a survey, correct, a survey of damage in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that's something that you were involved with yourself, as a member of Team Podkonje. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the order for the survey to be conducted asked each team to classify damages on buildings within your area of responsibility. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please pull up P63.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, if you could look at the first written paragraph that begins, "Reference," and I'll read the sentence below that. It says: "This HQ requires a survey of all teams AOR concerning number of houses destroyed or looted, minority people left behind, and HR violations, during HV Operation Storm or earlier." Now, I wanted to ask you, Mr. Tchernetsky, as far as you were aware, the part that says "or earlier" means that you were also tasked in your survey of damage to list damages which occurred from the period of 1992 to 1995, when the area was under the control of the authorities of the Republika Srpska Krajina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Earlier -- what I meant by that word "earlier" was that the damage that was inflicted upon buildings and harm that was caused to people by shelling prior to the operation, the period preceding the operation, which means July. Those were the shellings that were discussed in the first part of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that the term "or earlier" does not include a survey of damage of buildings or villages that were damaged or destroyed during the Serbian occupation of 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that every team's position, or was that just Team Podkonje's position?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all teams believed that to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you do agree with me, Mr. Tchernetsky, that there was damage to buildings, villages that occurred between 1992 and 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The damage was there. But when evaluating the damage, we did not include the destroyed buildings, prior damage, because it was obvious when it had been inflicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you exclude the prior damage?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We excluded it. We did not take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you determine what you considered to be a damaged building? What was the level of damage for a building to be noted "damaged"?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We divided damage into two main categories: Minor damage, that is, shrapnel damage do walls, shattered windows, and glass, on the one hand; and complete destruction, that is, damage that makes buildings unfit for use for habitation with structural damage to the walls, roof, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you determine whether or not something had been looted, how would you make that determination? What criteria would you use?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We entered these buildings, especially when touring villages and hamlets. We entered practically every house and observed what was inside and in what condition it was. We made these tours repeatedly, and we could see that initially a building was intact. Then after a while, the furniture and property inside was removed. Yet later, there was destruction inside, windows would be broken, things were partially burned inside, et cetera. That sort of damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there ever a survey conducted of what the damage was done to the buildings and villages separate and apart from the one that was done after Operation Storm? Maybe that was an unclear question. I will rephrase it. Was there a damage evaluation or report done by UNMO or anybody at UN HQ in Sector South of the damage that was done between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived into Sector South in end June. During my tenure, neither the team nor the headquarters received such assignments. What happened before me, I cannot know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, when you conducted your surveys, your damage surveys, did you have a form that you used, that you filled out for making your damage notations and assessments?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We got an approximate format, according to which we had to assess damage, and we worked with it. It consisted of three or four columns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Who gave you that format?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that a printed format?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the beginning, it was a verbal instruction. Later, a uniform form was developed in the course of our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how much later, after August 17th, 1995, a uniform form was -- started to be used?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. Maybe three or four days into it, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please pull up P65.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, is this the form that Team Podkonje used?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would this happen to be your handwriting on this form?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise whose handwriting it might be, from your Team Podkonje?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this how you would typically fill out one of these forms, your team?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How many of these forms do you estimate that you filled out?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: More than this one. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Such forms were filled in by every patrol upon completion of their mission every day, after they toured a certain area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in this particular form under section - it says number - but it is letter C: "DTG visited," and this is for Plavno. The last visit is noted as: "5, 1600 Bravo, September, 1995." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But there is no date on this particular document, other than the area was last visited on 5 September, 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see the date here. It's a working form that we were issued in order to make our daily report, and in order to compare if there was any damage inflicted later. That's why we have column C, date of the last prior visit until the present one, so as to enable us to compare.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's understood. But there is no date for what this present visit is on this sheet, P65. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not indicated. This is a working document of the patrol commander that was turned over to the officer on duty, so that he could make his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So just so I get an indication, you said that you were involved in helping and assisting in filling out P65. When you would go to Plavno and visit, for example, the village area in this P65, would all of you get together and then count the buildings? How was that done specifically?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would depend on how many vehicles we used when we went on mission. If we had one vehicle, we would drive up to a population centre, we would walk around, count, assess, and, later, we would sum things up. If we had several vehicles, two or more, we would divide the area into sectors to cover them jointly. All this data is not the work result of one person. It is the whole patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So, essentially, something like P65, if there was one vehicle, you would all put together everything on one document. But if there were more than one vehicle, is it fair to state that often there would be more than one document per visit?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This is the report of a patrol, of one patrol, and the patrol could consist of one, two, or three vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is fair to say, is it not, that at least on every patrol that you went after August 17th, 1995, if there was damage to be assessed, a form would be filled in on each patrol?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that at the beginning we didn't have these forms, and we worked according to instructions we were given; that is, complete damage, total damage, partial damage, looted buildings, et cetera. Later on, the headquarters developed these forms so that the output of all patrols and all teams would be uniform in assessing damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you ensure that the same building wasn't counted more than one time, in terms of partial or total damage?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried not to allow such things, but, of course, there is no -- there is no absolute guarantee that one and the same building wasn't counted twice, because there is all the human error and the human factor. All these are approximate figures, assessment, evaluation. As for the work of our team leaders, we didn't count in dozens. We went into every house. We assessed every single building, every structure, trying our best to be objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, I'd like you to -- to focus your attention now on the arrest and the hand over of the ARSK soldiers in Podinarje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: First, I'd like to refer to P130.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tchernetsky, P130 is an August 28th, 1995 sitrep that talks about this arrest and hand over of these ARSK soldiers, and I'd like to go over this with you in some detail. On page 1, under the highlights section, the highlights note that: "A large number of Serbs, including former RSK soldiers, are still hiding in the forests and mountains and wish to surrender." Now, you knew that, as far as late August of 1995, this was occurring throughout areas of Sector South, that there were former RSK soldiers still at large hiding in the forests and mountains. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. And in my practice, it was a unique case, when I found soldiers high in the mountains of Podinarje area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you, Mr. Tchernetsky. I asked you: Were you aware, on or about August 28th, that not just in Podinarje but in other areas of Sector South there were large numbers of ARSK soldiers who were hiding in the woods and mountains? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood you very well, and I can only say once again that I was not aware whether any soldiers were hiding all over Krajina or not. I knew only about that single case, when I found nine soldiers high up in the mountains of Podinarje. As to any other such cases, I had no such information, neither from the headquarters or any other source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So you were not aware of special police operations starting August 21st, 1995 throughout all different areas of the Sector South in which some of these ARSK soldiers were attempted to be captured?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of those operations until the very day, when it was planned to turn over those soldiers that I had found in the presence of other international organisations to Croatian authorities. And only that morning, prior to that operation, the Senior Military Observer of Sector South informed me that such a special operation would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, I don't think you understood my question. I didn't ask you about this specific date or this specific incident. I just asked you, in general, throughout Sector South, were you aware that the special police forces of the -- of the Ministry of Interior were conducting mop-up operations to find Serb soldiers throughout the forest? It is a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I think he has given a quite simple answer to that several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You moved from his awareness of soldiers, where he said, "I was aware only of these two," and that it was exceptional; and then you moved without further explanation to operations, apparently, as you said, in which some of these ARSK soldiers were attempted to be captured. Apparently, you are referring to soldiers. The witness told us he was not aware about. So by moving from one subject to another, mixing up things, matters do not become much clearer. Take it one by one. The witness has answered the question about his awareness of presence of soldiers. The witness has told us something about what he knew and what he was informed about special operations. So let's try to keep things simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I was trying to do, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me precisely what your responsibilities are when you find ARSK soldiers, or what your responsibilities were when you found them?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to specific responsibilities or special procedures when we found soldiers, we didn't have any. We had received no orders on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The sitrep, P130, I'd like you to go to page 6, please. Section E, "UNMO Team Podkonje reported ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, on this sitrep of August 28th, it says, at 1000 hours, you found four Serbs in the village of Milivojevici and six Serbs in the village Musica Stanovi, and that they asked the UNMOs to help them with food and to provide their transportation to the HQ Sector South refugee camp. On the next page, on the third line, it says: "UNMOs were informed that there was a group of former RSK soldiers hiding in the vicinity, and that they would like to lay down their weapons and start a civ," meaning civilian, "life." Now, were you -- I'd like to compare that to your statement, Mr. Tchernetsky, P204 on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to that, please, the very bottom of page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Approximately on 24-25 August 1995, during the patrol to the region of Podinarje, I found a small hamlet between Bukvin Stan and Musica Stanovi where remained several elderly Serbian families. I got information from the residents that several RSK soldiers were hiding," and on to page 5, "in the woods. With the help of the soldiers -- civilians, I met two of the soldiers and spoke to them." Now, your sitrep of August 28 is the first time that anything is ever mentioned about these ARSK soldiers. That's five days after August 24th, if you include the 24th as a date. Isn't that correct, Mr. Tchernetsky?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The thing is you are why now operating with some documents that I didn't have; and when I was making my statement, I was trying to remember after so many years how things were; but I couldn't, of course, remember precise dates. I had found them earlier. I stated that much. I tried to give them the possibility to leave the territory of Krajina, and I didn't report it to the headquarters. I admit that freely. Later on, when they attempted to get out and failed, and they returned, I talked to them, I explained the situation to them, and I organised their turnover to Croatian authorities with guarantees that their lives would be spared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, you started questioning whether he received instructions, what to do if you'd find ARSK soldiers. That question had been put witness by Mr. Russo. The question had been answered. He gave the same answer and you didn't give it any follow-up, so apparently that was not necessary. Now, the witness clearly stated in his statement that he did not immediately report, but only after a couple of days, after he first -- Now you put questions which do not bring, at least until to now, any new elements. If you want to emphasise that it was not immediately reported, the Bench knows that because we have read it, and it is clear there were a couple of days. Then to ask whether 28 August is five days after the other date, that is really not something that adds anything to what we know already. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, in your statement, P204, you did say that you didn't report them to the HQ, but you only reported to civilians in order to organise the humanitarian aid for them. You did not report the civilians in any of the sitreps before August 28th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably meant to say that I did not report the soldiers. I just don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: None of the sitreps from August 24 through August 27 contain any mention of providing humanitarian aid for civilians in this area, which means that you say in your statement that you reported about civilians, but you did not report that in any sitrep between August 24th through the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm to object to that. The testimony that's been in already and gone over several times is that the teams sent the sitrep to the HQ Sector South, the HQ Sector South sends its own sitrep to Zagreb. I think it is unfair to the witness to indicate that he didn't make a team report because it doesn't appear in the HQ Sector South sitrep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We, by now, know that sitreps are there at several levels. Providing humanitarian aid to civilians might not have been -- please focus on this because Mr Russo apparently is focussing more on the report. You are focussing on the content; that is, providing humanitarian aid to civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, I will answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment, one of our main tasks was to search for remaining Serbs in the territory of the former Serbian Krajina, to register them, in fact to record their needs, and poll them whether they want to stay in Krajina or leave. That's the information we were collecting at the time. That was our main task, and to turn over that information to international organisations and to headquarters. If people made any requests, we also tried to meet those requests as ordered by the headquarters, to provide food, to provide aid, to bring a doctor, et cetera. In that specific case, we were searching for people, we were registering them, and collecting information on what they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: None of the sitreps you discuss in those days talk about registering any people from this area, from August 24th to August 28th, do they? If we have to go through every single sitrep, Mr. Tchernetsky, I will it that, but I will represent to you that not one single sitrep from August 24th, 25th, 26th, or 27th, contains any information about humanitarian assistance for these people or the fact that you were registering them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, is there any dispute about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: There is no dispute about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The map that you brought to the soldiers, Mr Tchernetsky, that was a map that you brought with HV military positions, wasn't it, to help them escape capture?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. It was a blank map used by UNMOs. It was an absolutely blank map, only used for orientating yourself on the territory. As for Croatian military positions, I did not have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in your statement, it reads that you gave them a map, you showed them a possible route to Bosnia, and two days later you learned that the soldiers failed to get to Bosnia. That appears to be a clear attempt to assist them to escape to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic. I think, as a matter of fact, that most of these things are pretty clear. This Chamber is not seeking -- or, first of all, wants to hear about facts and not by the questioning of the witness to be subject of the apparent need of the parties to emphasise certain matters in full detail. I mean, what the meaning of it is, what the weight to be given is, is rather argumentative, and it's pretty obvious what happened here, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to just focus, Mr. Tchernetsky, on P130 again, page 7, the lower portion of that statement where it says, "At 1545 hours ..." This is again referring to the ARSK hand over. "Five young men of military age came inside the yard where UNMOs and HRAT were interviewing the civilians. They were civilians without arms. All of them are residents from the general area, Podinarje, and escaped from their units on 5th of August." My question to you, Mr. Tchernetsky, is: If these soldiers were all residents of the general area of Podinarje, why would you need to give them a map to get to Bosnia, when Podinarje is about five kilometres away from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they had never been there, in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Who told you that they had never been to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They lived in Podinarje. They were peasants, farmers before they were mobilised into the army. And when discussing the fact that they wanted to go to Bosnia, they told me that they didn't know how to get there, which roads to take to get there. One of them -- as far as I remember, I spoke to only one of those soldiers, and he could read the map, more or less. I gave him the map so that they could orient themselves and move accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, there's a map lying next to you in a binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Court, it is map 30 of the pack, and I would just like to use it for demonstrative purposes. And with the assistance of the usher, if we could put that on the ELMO. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, if you could take a look at the map and just point to Podinarje on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: For the benefit of the record. It's on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the area just above it, which is white, that's Bosnia and Herzegovina, is it not? Is that correct, Mr. Tchernetsky?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the border of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You can take that down now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, the sitrep of August 28th, where you start at -- where it starts at page 5 under "UNMO Team Podkonje" -- page 6, I'm sorry. Now, if you page through page 6 until the second-last page of that sitrep, the sitrep makes it appear that all of this happened in one day, on August 28th, meaning that they were found, that they were turned over, that everything happened in one day. But, in fact, it happened over the course of four days, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, do you find the fact that reporting this incident as one day in one sitrep, when it happened in fact in four days, do you think it was a bit deceptive?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, because this sitrep was compiled by the sector headquarters, and it summarizes the information that had been provided during several days. Yes. It summarizes the information that had arrived by certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the front page of the sitrep, it is called "UNMO HQ Sector South daily sitrep." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Tchernetsky, would you agree with me that the method in which these people were turned over endangered the lives of the civilians that were there, potentially?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did everything in order to avert any danger primarily to civilians and also to the lives of those soldiers. I saw simply no other solution under the circumstances --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as how to provide their security, safety, in the presence of international observers and representatives of international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the first of four days, you did not have them disarmed, did you? Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, let's just assume that the witness says "yes," then we can start over all the examination, the whole of the statement. It is not the first useless question you are putting. You apparently seek to emphasise the wrongdoings of this witness. I think that is not in dispute that he did not act within the mandate. And in order to explore all the details, not only to learn that Podkonje is five kilometres from the border, but then to see on the map where it is and then to see where the border is and that is really only four and a half kilometres even, that is not assisting the Chamber. Let's focus on core matters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you get the ICRC involved, Mr. Tchernetsky?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did involve representatives of the Red Cross and also representatives of the UNHCR, as well as representatives of the OSCE. But as you well know, representatives of the ICRC, according to their statute and mandate, did not take part in any joint operations. They always act independently. We simply provided to them the information on the fact that certain people were found in certain areas, and then they proceeded after that independently on their on. I don't remember whether they went out in the field with us or not, but the practice showed that representatives of the Red Cross never took part in joint operations. As for representatives of other organisations that were present in the UN camp, at the time were involved. I got them involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Ermolaev with you during one of the four days up at the -- up in the area?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Mr. Ermolaev was -- or, rather, worked at the headquarters, and this is where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we pull up P94, please, page 8, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, Mr. Ermolaev states in his statement, P94: "I do not remember an exact date; but in the same region, some eight, nine ARSK soldiers surrendered to an UNMO team which was sent for patrolling in the Dinara area." It identifies you as the Russian UNMO on the team. Then it says: "Having received initial report from Tchernetsky from the field, I moved there myself." So, at least, according to this statement, Mr. Ermolaev received a report from you, and came to that area where these soldiers were. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on that because I don't know about this. He didn't go there, at least not with me. I went there with members of my team: Pavel Komper, Peter Marti. I didn't travel there with Ermolaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I have asked this already. Mr. Ermolaev, in his statement, says that he received an initial report from you. Are you denying that you reported initially to him?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported to the headquarters, naturally. I reported through the deputy operations officer of the staff. All reports go through the deputy to the senior UNMO, and this is how he received the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, when you first found these soldiers, why didn't you report them to the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, it seems that you have not fully understood my previous guidance, isn't it? Just to continue in the way you do is not what I was giving you as guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you, Mr. Tchernetsky, to move to the latter part of your statement where you talk, on page 5 of P204, of another patrol you went on to Podinarje on the 30th and 31st of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could get to that portion of the statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, before we get into that portion of the statement, Mr. Tchernetsky, in none of the sitreps of August 30th or 31st is there contained any information about what is stated here in your statement. Is that a fair assessment? We could go over those sitreps, if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen them, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that there is nothing in those sitreps which are P132, P133, and P135, you would have no reason to disagree with me, would you?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask: Are these sitreps of the headquarters or of the UNMO team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: UNMO HQ, Sector South, daily sitrep.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely, such insignificant details were not included by the headquarters of the sector in their daily report. It depended on the senior UNMO, and his deputy, what was going to go in, in the sitrep. This information had to be included in the report submitted by our team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, I'm looking at the clock. We're close to a time we need a break. I asked you before the break how much time would you need. You said hour, hour and a half. And in view of the way in which you use your time, I'm going to strictly keep you to one hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just this section and then I am done, which probably take about ten, 15 minutes, and then I will be all done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will have another seven minutes, and we will have a break until ten minutes to one, and use your time as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Stevo Macakana, how do you know that person that you mentioned in your statement here, in P204?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how he introduced himself to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the first time that you met him?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was a member of the Serbian special police?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: He told me -- he told you he was a member of the Serbian special police?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you didn't indicate what member of what force he was with in your statement, Mr. Tchernetsky. It is it a pretty significant thing to meet a member of the Serbian special police in the Podinarje area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Serbian, but Croatian. This is an misunderstanding here. You are referring to Stevo Macakana. He is a representative of the Croatian special police - that is how he introduced himself to me - from a group called Dzi-Bu. That was by his own admission. That is what he told me, and I recorded that and I have that notation. But these are not Serbian special forces but, rather, Croatian special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's pull up 3D00-110 -- 3D00-0110, please. I put too many zeros. 3D00-110. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: My mistake, Your Honour. I apologise to the registrar and to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think this system is always eight digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is 3D00-0616 -- 0619. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, this document is a special report regarding criminal charges that were levelled against Mr. Macakana, who was a member of the military of the Serbian autonomous district of Krajina. Mr. Macakana was charged in November of 1992 with being involved in the killing of a Croatian civilian Milan Bulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you want to then put questions to the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Russo. No objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D218, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tchernetsky, Stevo Macakana, according to this information, was a member of the Serbian autonomous district militia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Anything is possible. I did not check his documents, and I wrote down information as he told me in the presence of another UNMO, Ivo Maknanaje [phoen]. He was the Czech captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Macakana was a Serbian person who was in the area of Podinarje. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Is this question directed to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. Tchernetsky.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Not Serbian. He was a member of a two-person team in a police -- in the Croatian police vehicle. He wore a uniform and had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in your statement, you said, on P204, on that patrol -- on page 5: "On that patrol in a place called Grabovica Drazica, I saw a group of special police headed by Stevo Macakana." A group -- you determined that a group is two people?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two people is a group. With them was one of the former soldiers that we had turned over to Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that soldier was released and he made it back to Podinarje, and he, Mr. Macakana, was trying to find his weapons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't released. These two policemen were supposed to escort him to the location where he, according to his own words, had left his weapons, because he was supposed to show them where the weapons, pick up the weapons, and go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were these special police headed by Stevo Macakana armed?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniform were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform. I don't know how else I can describe it to you. Just camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of the Croatian special police wore camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the operation in Podinarje was carried out with the participation of the military special police, I saw their members wearing this uniform at the time when these soldiers were turned over to Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, your seven minutes have become ten meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think we got a number for that document and it's been admitted, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, any objections against this document? Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're talking about the document of Stevo Macakana?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption, Your Honour. This becomes Exhibit D218.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D218 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the extra time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, we will have a break of 20 minutes. Who will be the first one after the break? Will it be you, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It will be me, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very well. We resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Cayley, who is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Mr. Cayley, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May it please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tchernetsky. I don't have many questions for you, but I would immediately like to you direct your mind to the subject matter which you were speaking about before the break and that is the discovery and arrest of the nine ARSK soldiers. Now, do you recall in your evidence this morning you stated that the soldiers were turned over to the Croatian authorities? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You stated that one was released?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that you had heard that the others, the other eight, were convicted, yes; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about what the court decided. They were in -- remanded in custody. They were detained in a school house. While they were in that school house, they were visited by the human rights team and representatives of the Red Cross, and it was from them that I learned that these people were transferred to Zadar; or to prison in Zadar, possibly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could we have Defence Exhibit 100, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'd just like to very briefly, Mr. Tchernetsky, show you the criminal report that is actually related to exactly what you're talking about. Now, in you look at the document in front of you, it says "6th of June, 1995" in the English translation; but, in fact, in you look at the original version, it is, in fact, the "06.06.95". So that is a mistake. So the document does not date from 6 June 1995. It dates from 6 September 1995. You see, it is a criminal report from the Zadar-Knin police administration. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I don't think it is disputed between the parties that the names listed there are eight of the soldiers that were concerned in these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But if we could please go to the last page -- I'm sorry, the page before last. I apologise. There's a big space. The prior page to that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if you could just read the final paragraph, I think this will shed some more light on what you were discussing. So the final paragraph on that page. Have you read that, Mr. Tchernetsky?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: A very straightforward question for you: Were you aware at this time that the Zadar-Knin police administration was the superior police headquarters of the Knin police station, so the police station located in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question and then they'll see whether the witness received interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The question was this: Were you aware at this time, in August and September of 1995, that the Zadar-Knin police administration was the superior police headquarters for the local police station that was based in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, equally, you were not aware that it was the Zadar-Knin police administration that was responsible for the investigation of serious crimes in the region?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. We can move to the next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I would to now direct your mind, please, Mr. Tchernetsky, to the episode that you described taking place sometime between the 10th and the 12th of August of 1995. This was the fire that you say that you observed in Knin. Can you direct your mind to that for me, please. What I'd like to try and do this in respect of this event -- and if you wish you can actually turn to page 3 of your first statement. That's Prosecution Exhibit 204, and it is, in fact, the last paragraph on page 3 of that statement concerning these events. Now, you estimate that this particular event took place sometime between the 10th and 12th of August, 1995. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the precise date but it was somehow just after I returned from leave at the beginning of my tenure, when our group, our team, was stationed in the same place as the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, do you have your statement in front of you at the moment? Do you have that page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you go to the last three lines of that paragraph. Do you see that it concerns the renting of an office, of a house for your office needs, from a lady whose name has been redacted, and it gives her phone number; and then it says that her apartment in Cara Lazara Sinska Cesta was looted and set on fire. Now, did that event, did the renting of that new office happen around about the same time as the observation of this fire in the centre of Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The apartment was burned down later, after we rented a new office and after we moved there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days later --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You misunderstood my question. I'm interested in the actual renting of the office. Did the renting of the new office, the acquisition of your new premises, take place around about the same time that you observed the fire in the centre of Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were renting that office. But for security reasons, many of the members of our team refused to be there during the night. And as a rule, only three our four people were on duty there by night during the first days, while the rest were at the base. It's approximately those same days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, we could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 118.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tchernetsky, you can see that this is an UNMO's report dated the 13th of August of 1995, and that it covers the period from 0001, so one minute past 12.00 on the 12th of August, to 2000 hours on the 13th of August. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to the final page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There you will see in the final paragraph that your team, Team Podkonje, reported during this period, and I'm actually interested in the last paragraph, which is "Admin." I guess admin stands for administration. Yes? Sorry. I realise I am asking you in English, and it's being translated --

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, administrative. Administrative issues, administrative affairs. Nothing to do with operations, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you see there that it refers to your team moving into new team accommodation. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is it likely that you reported that matter to the duty officer at Team Podkonje?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the team commander who reported, and the duty officer. At that time, I was not the commander of team.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And do you see that it also says that the landlady, this old Serbian lady, was protected by her Croat neighbours when the Croat offensive moved into Knin? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that, and I can confirm it. It was really so. She said so herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to say that the latest time that could you have seen this fire, based on the information in this report, was perhaps sometime on the 13th of August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember any precise dates, I did not keep a diary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It appears, Mr. Cayley, that you seem to draw some conclusions from the information until now. I heard the witness say that when they moved into that new building or that new premises, that only a few stayed there overnight and then overs stayed in the UN compound. I also understand from his testimony, the earlier parts of it, that they moved from the UN compound and were stopped, more or less, where you crossed the railroad. Now, if it is about logic, then I have difficulties to follow your logic, because part of the team would stay in the UN compound and the other part would be -- If it's not logic then, let's ask the witness what he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think -- well, you've misunderstood me, so I must have misled the Court. What I was trying to establish is exactly the end day on which he could observed the event. And if you look at the statement, you will see that he refers to this particular event after the observation of the fire, the event of renting the new accommodation. So, in that sense, this would have provided an end date, or and end time and an end date, to when he could have observe the fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well is that, as you say, in his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you go to his statement, Your Honour, page 3, final three lines, you will see that he refers to this event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "I know from her that her apartment ..." You asked a question about that, and he said that was later. That it was her apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a lot of confusion. I have really have difficulties in following, if it is about logic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the actual observation of the fire itself, Mr. Tchernetsky, did you select that particular route that day for yourself, or were you ordered to go on that route, to patrol around Knin town centre?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We set out directly towards the site of fire. That was the shortest way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you decided yourself to go on that day. You weren't ordered to go by your team commander?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I received an assignment, but I chose the route myself because it was the most direct and the shortest route.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, on the first occasion, when you tried to observe the fire, you were stopped at a check-point. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the centre of town, near the railroad bridge, we were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you were stopped by military police. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were stopped by civilian police, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If could I have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, on the second occasion, when you observed the fire, were there military police officers present or civilian police officers present?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say who was wearing the camouflage uniform, was it the military police or soldiers; but there was also civilian police, together with the fire brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's go back your first statement, which is P204, and it's the final paragraph of page 3. And if you go halfway down, you will see it begins: "We managed to approach the site from the other side of Knin. Tor took the camera and started taking pictures when I was talking to the military police officers." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And is that right? Were you talking to a military police officer?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably not an officer. One or two persons, one or two men in uniform, approached me when they saw our vehicle. It was not a long conversation. We just pretended that we had lost our way, we asked for directions, they showed us the way, and that was enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now look at P205, which is the second statement, Prosecutor's Exhibit 205 of the 6th of December, 2007. And, please, if we could about to paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you will see in the second sentence, it states: "I recall this location as the railway bridge. Marked as 3 on annex AT-3 is the location of the block of houses that we could see burning when we were stopped by the military police. I know they were military police because their vehicles indicated so." Do you now recall identifying these military police because the vehicles had insignia which demonstrated that they were military police?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, it's hard to say now. I see the discrepancy between my statements from 2002 and 2007. I find it hard to -- to remember now and to state clearly whether it was military police or civilian police. But they were police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've given a number of different descriptions of the nature of the fire. Today, you referred to the entire neighbourhood was practically on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that, Mr. President, is at page 25, line 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In your first statement, you say the following, and I will read it to you. It's the fourth -- the third sentence, actually, on the last paragraph of page 3. I'll read it to. If you wish to find it, you can. "We went by car directly to the centre of Knin where we saw the whole part of the town on fire?" Then, in your second statement, Prosecution Exhibit 205, you give a slightly different description again, in that you say, at the second sentence of paragraph 16: "Marked as 3 on annex AT-3 is the location of the block of houses that we could see burning when we were stopped by the military police." How many houses do you recall burning at this time?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say because it was night. A number of houses were on fire. This whole territory was surrounded by people and by vehicles. But when I was saying "neighbourhood," I understood it to mean a block, a block of low houses, one or two floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So are we speaking about one house or two houses, and can you give me a number, please?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not less than ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Not less than ten houses. Now, you said earlier today that all significant events would be reported up the chain to UNMO headquarters in Knin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the burning of ten -- up to ten houses, you would accept, as a significant event, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's take a very brief look. I'm not going to show you the UNMO reports that don't actually mention anything described by Team Podkonje, but I will show you a number of the reports during this period which address burnings of houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So if we could please have Prosecutor's Exhibit 116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about ten houses burning not being in the sitrep.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The Chamber is aware that individual houses being burned appear in many sitreps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just show him two sitreps, which actually describe the events that were being addressed by this team at the moment. It will be very brief. I will be finished before the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. May I take it that your reference to page 25, line 19 was page 23, line 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This, you can see, Mr. Tchernetsky, is a report from UNMO headquarters Sector South, P116, and it addresses the time-period between 1800 hours on 10 August and 1800 hours on the 11th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we could please go to page 11 of this report, last two digits 11 -- it's page 3. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you look at paragraph 8, you will see that the only thing that Team Podkonje reported to the UNMO team headquarters was the issue of a patrol trying to repair a radio repeater. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to object to that. The question is not a fair characterise. It indicates only that that's what HQ reported from Team Podkonje's report, not that that's the only thing that Team Podkonje reported to the HQ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you put it in such a way that it reflects --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, do you see that here is reported by Team Podkonje the fact that a patrol was sent with a radio technician to a radio repeater? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that. I see that. However, that was only during the last day, between the 10th and 11th. I re-emphasise that I do not remember the exact date when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm also right in saying that restrictions on movement that affected UNMO patrols were also affected, weren't they, to UNMO headquarters by all of the teams. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if you look at the bottom to of this page, you will see here "restrictions on movement." Do you --

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. I'm --

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th, it mentions only the relocation of the administrative patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. If you could direct your attention to this particular report. I just want you to look at where it mentions "restrictions of movement" at the end of this report. You will see that the only thing that the Podkonje team reports, in serial 1, is that the fact that they needed written permission to go to the Promine repeater station. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And there is no report, is there, on restrictions of movement affecting Team Podkonje in the centre of Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that on the 10th, between the 10th and 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's now look at P117, Prosecutor's Exhibit 117, which covers the period that you want to refer to. Now, this, Mr. Tchernetsky, you will see is a report from the 11th of August at 1800 hours to the 12 of August at 1800 hours. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we could please turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you'll see there --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, the page could be moved down, and if, please, the UNMO Team Podkonje reported part could be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you can see there, Mr. Tchernetsky, what was reported for that period of time, the period of time 11th August, 1800 hours, to 12 August, 1800 hours. You will see here that Team Podkonje observed a burning house on the 12th of August at 1645 hours. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that. I have to reiterate that I don't remember the exact date, so I can't really say why. At least, I don't see this incident reflected in these two reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you would accept that if a single burning house was regarded as significant to report, then ten houses on fire would have been even more significant, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tchernetsky, Mr. Munkelien has already given evidence in these proceedings, and he did not arrive in Knin until the 14th of August of 1995. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact chronology, but I know for a fact that he was with us. That means that this may have happened later, not on the 10th, but, say, the 12th, the 15th, the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look, then, at Prosecutor's Exhibit 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if, please, we could go to page 2, and if, please, we could go to paragraph 9, and if that could be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you can take it from me that this is the first indication in any UNMO report of you being on patrol with Major Munkelien, and he is referred to there by his first name, Major Tor. You can see that's on the 17th of August.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you can see here that the team observed one burning house in Knin town, only 200 metres from the team's new office accommodation.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is it possible that you may be confusing events, Mr. Tchernetsky, and that this is, in fact, what you think you observed between the 10th and the 12th of August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I insist that I saw a major fire; in fact, not less than a block was burning. It was in the late evening hours after dark, and that was in August. Now, as to the exact date, I really wouldn't be able to say. But I'm sure about the fact, and I'm sure about the location where this was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any further questions to ask this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. There is an little time left. Would you have a subject, Mr. Kehoe, that could be dealt with in three minutes to start with?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, not really, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tchernetsky, we have to adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow, the 21st of May, at 9.00 in the morning. But I would ask, Madam Usher first to escort you out of the courtroom. I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given, and we'll certainly finish your testimony tomorrow. Would you please follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to give the parties some guiding on how to deal with non-reported matters in sitreps. There are apparently two situations: The one where there's no reporting, and another more specific case where this is a risk of confusing an event that appears in the testimony with an event that was reported by different day, different area, perhaps, different details. Now, if it is just about not reporting, if a witness says, Something happened to me between 10th and 17th of August, then the parties are invited to agree on whether this events appears in the report, yes or no. If not, we don't have to go through all of this. You just put to the witness that the parties have reviewed the sitreps, and then you should detail a report by whom, to whom, so that we don't have the different level of reporting problems. That can be put to the witness, and then the witness can be asked whether he has an explanation for the non-appearance of this event. That, of course, would be different, if there's, I would say, not an invented risk but objectively supported risk of confusion, in which case, of course, the attention can be drawn to the event that was reported, and then ask the witness as, I think, in the second instance Mr. Cayley did, whether there was any risk that he may have confused two events. That might save some time. Of course, this is based on the assumption that the parties would sit together prior to the testimony of the witness, where the Defence wants to draw our attention to the fact that a certain matter was not reported. At the same time, these events, of course, I take it, are taken from the 92 ter statement of the witness or from the summary of his testimony. So, if it was not reported, I don't think that it would reveal a great secret if the Defence, under those circumstances, would address the Prosecutor and ask whether the Prosecution agrees that in none of the sitreps at whatever level this event was reported. That might save some time in court. We stand adjourned until tomorrow, the 21st day of May, at 9.00 a.m.
